newsitem.title: FRANCE: Peugeot may cut workers if retirement plan fails.
newsitem.headline: Peugeot may cut workers if retirement plan fails.

text.p: French carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen may have to lay off workers if the government does not agree to an early retirement plan proposed by the French car industry, chairman Jacques Calvet said on Wednesday.

"If they force us to lay off workers, which we might have to, it would cost less than early retirements, and I would do it because I wouldn't have a choice," Calvet told reporters after a news conference at the Citroen branch's headquarters.
He said the industry's outlook was grim, with French sales expected to fall between nine and 10 percent next year to 1.93 million cars while the European market would probably be flat.

Calvet did not say how many jobs needed to be cut. But French newspapers reported last month that he and Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer were seeking government approval for 40,000 early retirements over five years in exchange for hiring 14,000 young workers.
This would address high youth unemployment in France and lower the average age of staffs at both countries, which is above 40.
The PSA group employs 139,900 people, including 112,200 in France. Renault employs 139,950, including 99,884 in France.

"We told the government we were under severe constraints, and we envisaged staff reductions under acceptable conditions," Calvet said. Early retirement packages are more generous than layoffs, and more expensive.

"We also asked for a review of the breakdown in contributions for early retirement which isn't good now, as the proportion paid by companies has risen sharply in relation to that paid by the state and by workers," he said.
In recent years, the employer's share of the cost for early retirement has quadrupled to 16 percent, with the employee's share steady at three percent, and the rest paid by the state.

The difficulty with the carmakers' proposal, Calvet said, was that it would present the government with a big bill at a time when it was tightening its belt as part of a drive for European monetary union. It also risked setting a precedent for other industries seeking relief.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra last month appointed a retired car industry executive, Bernard Cabaret, to study the proposal and turn in a report in January.
Borotra also urged Renault and the PSA group to study other ways to cut costs and become more competitive, for instance by cooperating more in joint ventures and production.

For 29 of the past 34 months, the government has underpinned the car market in France by offering incentives for people to buy new cars for old. The last scheme expired on September 30 and the government has not discussed new aid, although officials say they are closely watching the industry's performance.
